title: Lesson 79: Human Oversight: Dashboards, Approvals, Kill Switches, and Escalation Design
description: How to build oversight that actually controls an agent: dashboards that show agent behavior rather than infrastructure, approval gates that classify risk deterministically and sit in the authorization path, kill switches that revoke authority instead of pausing a process, and escalation paths with a named owner, a clock, and a safe default.

questions.question: A team builds an LLM-based risk classifier to decide which agent actions need human approval, and feeds it the same user request and retrieved documents the agent saw. Per lesson 79, what is the problem?
options: An LLM classifier is too slow for a real-time approval path

The classifier reads the same untrusted content as the request being evaluated, so adversarial text can influence it into marking the request low-risk; risk classification should be deterministic policy logic as the authoritative signal, with LLM-assisted classification only as optional input that a deterministic layer re-checks
An LLM classifier cannot output a risk tier without fine-tuning
There is no problem as long as the classifier runs on a separate model from the agent
questions.explanation: The lesson follows AWS guidance that risk classification cannot rely on an LLM exposed to the same untrusted content as the request being evaluated, because adversarial content could influence the classifier into marking the request as low-risk. Deterministic logic (policy engines, rule-based classifiers) is the authoritative signal; LLM-assisted classification is an optional input a deterministic layer re-checks.

questions.question: An operations agent starts making anomalous writes at 2am. The on-call engineer wants to kill it. Which sequence does lesson 79 prescribe, and why that order?
options: Stop the container, then page the team, then look at logs later
Revoke the credentials first, then capture the snapshot, and skip notifying dependents to avoid panic

Capture a forensic snapshot of memory, active sessions, and pending operations, then revoke credentials (deny-all on the role while preserving it), then broadcast the quarantine event so dependent workflows trip their circuit breakers; evidence comes first because recovery destroys it, and authority is what actually stops the agent
Pause new intake and let in-flight tasks finish, which is sufficient containment for any anomaly
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the order as snapshot, revoke, notify. Evidence first because recovery destroys it, authority second because permissions are the real capability, notification third so downstream workflows can activate circuit breakers. It also names two anti-patterns: quarantine by stopping the process without revoking credentials (the agent restarts with the same reach), and relying on a human to trigger quarantine at all.

questions.question: A finance team reviews 150 agent-proposed payments a day. Six weeks in, the approval log shows most decisions complete in under five seconds, and one bad payment gets approved by a reviewer who says they 'assumed the queue was pre-checked.' Which fix matches lesson 79?
options: Add a second approval step for every payment, since more review means more safety
Remove the queue entirely and let the agent pay autonomously, since reviewers clearly are not adding value
Trust the reviewers, because a five second decision is normal for an experienced specialist

Treat the fast approvals as a fatigue signal: risk-tier the gate so only actions where judgment changes the outcome need review, put the action, reason, actor, effect, evidence and confidence on the approval card so a genuine refusal is possible, and log reviewer identity and timestamps so the gate can be audited
questions.explanation: The lesson treats the share of approvals completed in a few seconds as the cheapest rubber-stamp detector, and describes rubber-stamping as the predictable result of routing more through review than judgment requires. The fixes it prescribes are risk-tiered approval, enough context on the review screen for a reviewer to genuinely say no (the action, reason, actor, effect), and logged decisions with reviewer identity and timestamps. Adding a second step to everything deepens the fatigue rather than fixing it.
